title: “Stand Still and See the Salvation of the Lord” — Sometimes Faith Stands Still Before God Says Move
paragraphs: “Stand Still and See the Salvation of the Lord” — Sometimes Faith Stands Still Before God Says Move
There are moments when everything inside you screams, “Do something.”
Fix it.
Call somebody.
Send the message.
Defend yourself.
Make the decision.
Run.
Fight.
Explain.
Force the door open.
Anything but stand there.
Because standing still can feel like weakness when your heart is racing.
It can feel irresponsible when the bills are waiting.
It can feel foolish when the doctor’s words are still echoing in your mind.

It can feel unbearable when your marriage is trembling, your family is fractured, your prayers seem unanswered, your future is uncertain, and the thing you thought God was going to rescue you from appears to be getting closer.
Sometimes the hardest thing God can ask of a frightened human heart is not to fight.
Not to flee.
Not to manufacture a miracle.
Just...
stand.
That is where Israel found itself.
Behind them was Egypt.
In front of them was the sea.
And somewhere between the two stood a terrified people who had been delivered from slavery but had not yet learned how to live like people who were free.
They could hear Pharaoh coming.
Imagine that sound.
The thunder of horses.
The grinding of chariot wheels.
The shouting of soldiers.
The dust rising behind them.
And before them?
Water.
No bridge.
No visible escape.
No military advantage.
No human solution.
They had obeyed God and somehow obedience had led them to a place that looked impossible.
That detail matters.
Because sometimes we quietly assume that if we are following God, every road should immediately make sense.
Then life corners us.
And suddenly we wonder whether we heard God at all.
Maybe that is where you are.
You prayed.
You tried to obey.
You walked away from what God told you to leave.
You stopped going back to the thing that was destroying you.
You believed God for something better.
And now you are standing somewhere between what God brought you out of and what He has not yet opened in front of you.
Egypt is behind you.
The sea is ahead of you.
And fear is whispering:
“Go back.”
That is the moment Exodus 14 becomes more than an ancient story.
It becomes painfully personal.
The Israelites cried to Moses:
“Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us to the desert to die?”
Fear had already rewritten their memory.
Slavery suddenly looked safer than uncertainty.
Bondage began to feel more comfortable than dependence upon God.
And we still do this.
We ask Jesus to free us, but when freedom becomes frightening, yesterday’s chains start looking strangely familiar.
The old relationship.
The old addiction.
The old compromise.
The old bitterness.
The old secret sin.
The old version of ourselves.
At least we knew how Egypt worked.
But faith sometimes brings you to a shoreline where returning to Egypt feels easier than trusting God with the sea.
Then Moses speaks words that frightened people desperately needed to hear:
“Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the deliverance the LORD will bring you today.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking.
אַל־תִּירָאוּ הִתְיַצְּבוּ וּרְאוּ אֶת־יְשׁוּעַת יְהוָה
’Al-tira’u, hityatzevu, u-re’u et-yeshu‘at YHWH.
“Do not fear. Stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD.”
That word translated “salvation” or “deliverance” is יְשׁוּעָה — yeshu‘ah.
Deliverance.
Rescue.
Salvation.
Moses was not telling Israel to admire its own courage.
He was directing terrified eyes away from Pharaoh, away from the sea, away from their own inability...
and toward the saving action of God.
Then comes one of Scripture’s most unforgettable declarations:
יְהוָה יִלָּחֵם לָכֶם וְאַתֶּם תַּחֲרִישׁוּן
YHWH yilachem lakhem, ve’atem tacharishun.
“The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.”
Exodus 14:14.
Read that again.
The LORD will fight for you.
There are battles where frantic human striving cannot accomplish what only God can do.
There are accusations you cannot answer enough.
People you cannot change.
Doors you cannot force open without damaging yourself.
Hearts you cannot manipulate into loving you.
Outcomes you cannot control.
Seas you cannot split.
And maybe part of your exhaustion comes from trying to perform God’s part in the story.
You have been fighting as though everything depends on you.
Thinking until two in the morning.
Replaying conversations.
Imagining disasters that have not happened.
Trying to control everybody’s perception of you.
Checking your phone again.
And again.
And again.
Trying to rescue yourself from tomorrow before tomorrow has even arrived.
But hear the Word of God:
“The LORD will fight for you.”
Standing still does not mean God has abandoned you.
Silence does not mean heaven has stopped working.
Waiting does not mean your story has ended.
And yet we need to keep reading, because biblical faith is not passive fatalism.
Immediately after Israel is told to stand firm, God says to Moses:
“Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward.”
Exodus 14:15.
There it is.
First:
Stand.
Then:
Move.
There was a moment when panic needed to stop.
Then there was a moment when feet needed to move.
And wisdom is knowing the difference.
Sometimes faith refuses to move before God says move.
Sometimes faith refuses to remain where God says go.
Both can be obedience.
Standing still is not the same thing as doing nothing forever.
It is refusing to let fear become your commander.
It is refusing to run back to Egypt merely because the sea has not opened yet.
It is becoming quiet enough before God that when He says, “Move,” fear no longer gets the deciding vote.
Some of us keep asking God to bless a movement He never commanded.
We rush because waiting exposes how little control we actually possess.
We send the message because silence makes us uncomfortable.
We enter relationships because loneliness frightens us.
We make financial decisions because anxiety tells us that immediate action must be better than patient wisdom.
We retaliate because surrender feels humiliating.
We call impulsiveness “faith” because waiting on God feels too vulnerable.
But Scripture repeatedly confronts our addiction to control.
Psalm 46:10 says:
הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים
Harpu u-de‘u ki anokhi Elohim.
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
The Hebrew verb הַרְפּוּ — harpu carries the sense of letting go, ceasing, relaxing one’s grip.
That changes the picture.
“Be still” is not merely God telling nervous people to sit quietly.
There is a surrender in it.
Release your grip.
Stop acting as though the universe remains intact because you are holding it together.
Know that I am God.
Not you.
That sentence can wound our pride before it heals our anxiety.
Because many of us want God to give us peace without asking us to surrender control.
We want Him to calm the sea while leaving our hands wrapped around the steering wheel.
But sometimes the mercy of God is that He brings us somewhere our strength finally admits:
“I cannot save myself.”
And that is where the Gospel begins to shine.
Because the deepest sea in front of humanity was never merely financial trouble, rejection, heartbreak, sickness, disappointment, or uncertainty.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Scripture does not flatter us about this.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
We have not merely been wounded by a broken world.
We have participated in its brokenness.
We have sinned against the God who made us.
We have loved things more than Him.
Trusted ourselves more than Him.
Hidden what we were ashamed to confess.
Called darkness harmless because admitting the truth would require repentance.
And there is no human strategy capable of opening a road through that sea.
Religion cannot purchase forgiveness.
Good deeds cannot erase guilt.
Money cannot buy reconciliation with God.
An offering cannot purchase grace.
No ministry can stand between you and God as your Savior.
Only Jesus Christ can.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings climbing their way toward God.
It is the astonishing announcement that God came for sinners.
Jesus entered our world.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed the rejected.
Touched the unclean.
Confronted hypocrisy.
Called sinners to repentance.
Loved His enemies.
And then He walked deliberately toward the cross.
The One who had no sin was treated as condemned.
The innocent One carried the shame of the guilty.
Jesus was crucified.
Buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
The cross looked like the end.
It was not.
The tomb looked final.
It was not.
The disciples thought the story had collapsed into scandal, humiliation, grief, and death.
Then Sunday came.
That is what Jesus does.
He walks into stories we thought were over and writes resurrection where we expected only an ending.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From bondage to freedom.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But grace is not permission to remain in Egypt.
Jesus does not merely forgive us so that we can comfortably return to the chains He died to break.
The Gospel calls us to repent.
To turn.
To surrender.
To believe.
To follow Christ.
Maybe that is the word somebody reading this has been avoiding.
Repent.
Not because God delights in crushing sinners.
Because Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
You do not need to clean yourself up enough to become worthy of the cross.
You come because you are not worthy.
That is why it is grace.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the dishonesty.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you desperately hope nobody discovers.
Stop hiding in Egypt while pretending you are walking toward the Promised Land.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
There is mercy at the feet of Jesus.
Perhaps you are reading this while facing a different kind of sea.
You already belong to Christ, but you are exhausted.
You have prayed the same prayer so many times that you barely know what else to say.
Nothing seems to be changing.
And somewhere deep inside, you have begun interpreting God’s silence as God’s absence.
Do not confuse the two.
At the Red Sea, God had not abandoned Israel because the road was invisible.
The road simply had not been revealed yet.
The Israelites could not see a highway beneath the water.
They saw an obstacle.
God saw a path.
They saw Pharaoh.
God saw an enemy whose pursuit would not have the final word.
They saw a dead end.
God saw a place where generations would remember His deliverance.
The sea did not need to disappear for God to be faithful.
It needed to obey Him.
What looks impossible to you is still under the authority of God.
That does not mean every painful circumstance will end exactly as we want.
Biblical faith is not a promise that Christians receive every outcome they request.
Sometimes God delivers us from suffering.
Sometimes He sustains us through suffering.
Sometimes the answer arrives quickly.
Sometimes faithfulness means enduring while trusting promises we will not see completed in this life.
Our confidence is not that God must obey our preferred ending.
Our confidence is that in Christ, suffering, sin, death, and hell do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
So maybe you do not need another frantic plan tonight.
Maybe you need to stop.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Seek wise, godly counsel.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Wait where God has not yet given clarity.
And when His Word makes the next faithful step clear...
move.
Not because the sea no longer looks frightening.
Because the One leading you is greater than the sea.
There is another detail in Exodus that I cannot escape.
Israel had to walk through.
God opened the way, but they still had to step into it.
Imagine that first step.
Walls of water on either side.
The ground beneath their feet.
Egypt behind them.
Freedom ahead.
I wonder how many trembling feet crossed that night.
Faith is not always fearless.
Sometimes faith is a shaking foot taking the next obedient step because God has spoken.
Maybe that is you.
You are still afraid.
Still healing.
Still grieving.
Still tempted.
Still uncertain.
But you have not gone back to Egypt.
That matters.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail.
God knows the story behind those three words.
That is what the body of Christ should look like.
Not perfect people performing perfection.
Redeemed people pointing one another toward a perfect Savior.
And if this article brought someone to your mind, do not keep it to yourself.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Send it to the family member who has stopped talking about what hurts.
Send it to the believer whose faith has become tired.
Send it even to the seeker who does not yet know what to do with Jesus.
One shared truth can arrive in somebody’s life at an hour you knew nothing about.
There may come a night when you are the one who needs to remember:
Do not fear.
Stand firm.
See the salvation of the LORD.
Then, when God says move...
move.
But hear this carefully because truth matters more than conversion numbers:
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

Support should therefore come freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and never from spiritual pressure. Scripture teaches the principle plainly: “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So if you want to glorify God with your resources, begin with faithful stewardship according to Scripture.
Free resources.
Scripture.
Discipleship.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Tools designed to help keep Christ at the center.
Not to build a crowd around us.
To keep pointing a crowd beyond us...
to Jesus.
Because one day every platform disappears.
Every follower count becomes irrelevant.
Every possession changes hands.
Every human voice grows silent.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself the question Israel had to face at the edge of the sea:
What has fear been telling me to run back to?
What “Egypt” keeps calling my name whenever following God becomes uncomfortable?
What am I trying to control because I am afraid to trust God?
And what has God already made clear that I now need to obey?
Be honest.
Someone standing before their own Red Sea may need to hear what God did in yours.
Follow.
But whatever you do, do not mistake the messenger for the Savior.
We cannot split your sea.
We cannot forgive your sin.
We cannot resurrect your soul.
We can only point toward the One who can save.
His name is Jesus.
And perhaps that is what you needed to remember tonight.
You are staring at the water, wondering where the road went.
God never promised you would always see the road before obedience.
Sometimes faith stands still before God says move.
Sometimes you will hear the chariots before you see the pathway.
Sometimes your hands will shake.
Sometimes your prayers will come out as tears.
Sometimes all you will have is enough strength to whisper His name.
Jesus.
And sometimes that is where the story begins to turn.
Because the sea in front of you does not get to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
